bib.title: Agent Laboratory: Using LLM Agents as Research Assistants

read.skipped: Survey-form appendix (C) and reference list skimmed; result tables (Figs 5-9) are images with no text layer, values taken from the earlier legacy read of rendered pages and marked in notes.

question: Can a pipeline of LLM agents with optional human feedback carry a human-given ML research idea through literature review, experiments and a written report cheaply and at useful quality?
hypothesis: Human feedback at each stage improves research quality, and a specialised solver (mle-solver) beats existing ML-agent solvers.
contributions: Open-source LLM agent framework (Agent Laboratory), compute flexible, for ML research
Human evaluation of papers across experiment quality, report quality, usefulness by backend (gpt-4o, o1-mini, o1-preview)
NeurIPS-style evaluation showing a gap between human and automated reviewer scores
Co-pilot mode evaluated on custom and preselected topics
Cost and time statistics per phase and backend ($2.33 per paper with gpt-4o)
mle-solver on a MLE-Bench subset outperforming MLAB, OpenHands and AIDE

method.summary: Three-phase pipeline (literature review via arXiv, experimentation with mle-solver, report writing with paper-solver) run by role-prompted agents (PhD, Postdoc, ML Engineer, SW Engineer, Professor) on top of off-the-shelf LLMs. mle-solver iteratively EDITs/REPLACEs Python code scored by an LLM reward model; paper-solver does the same for LaTeX scored by an automated NeurIPS-style reviewer. Evaluated by human surveys, runtime stats and MLE-Bench.
method.task: Autonomous and co-pilot ML research (idea to code and report)

datasets.name: MLE-Bench (subset)
datasets.split: inputs: 80% train / 20% dev random split of original training set; final code evaluated on Kaggle test set
datasets.preprocessing: Data placed into numpy arrays instead of file paths; solver given Kaggle description and distilled knowledge from Kaggle notebooks

datasets.name: Five research-question templates
datasets.source: authors' own: cognitive biases; ViT vs CNN pixel noise; MedQA differential diagnosis; word order in multiple choice; gender role play on math

datasets.name: HuggingFace datasets
datasets.source: searchable by ML Engineer via search HF command

other.note: same model also used as AIDE backend baseline

inference.temperature: Agent 0.8 (lit review); score generation 0.6; repair 0.8; initial code 1.0; mle-solver 1.0; paper-solver initial paper 0.8, solver 1.0
inference.samples: one paper per topic x backend (15 autonomous); 10 raters x 3 papers; MLE-Bench run counts not stated ('several runs' for comparators)
inference.prompting: Role prompts, phase prompts, command prompts (Appendix B); history line per step; at 70% of steps a 'finish and submit' string is appended
inference.retrieval: arXiv API: summary action returns top 20 abstracts; Table 1: 5 paper summaries, full-text history decay 3 steps

parameters.experiment timeout: 120 s data prep, 600 s running experiments

other.hardware: 2023 MacBook Pro, Apple M3 Max, 36 GB memory (Appendix A.2)
other.automated reviewer: Adapted from Lu et al. 2024b NeurIPS reviewer; reviewer backbone not stated here
other.paper length target: 8 pages or ~4000 words; 8 sections; max 2 figures

metrics.name: Human experiment/report quality and usefulness
metrics.definition: Survey rating 1-5 by volunteer PhD students

metrics.name: NeurIPS-style criteria
metrics.definition: Quality, significance, clarity, soundness, presentation, contribution on 1-4; overall 1-10

metrics.name: MLE-Bench medals / above median human
metrics.definition: Kaggle medals and human-median comparison on test set

baselines: The AI Scientist cost (~$15, from Lu et al.)
eval.protocol: Human surveys (Appendix C): 10 volunteer PhD raters for autonomous papers; co-pilot self and external evaluation; no significance tests, CIs or SDs reported; number of co-pilot researchers/externals not stated; raters told papers are AI generated

prompts.text: You are a professor agent who is serving as an expert reward model that can read a research plan, research code, and code output and are able to determine how well a model followed the plan, built the code, and got the proper output scored from 0 to 1 as a float.
You must finish this task and submit as soon as possible!
Your method MUST not get 0% accuracy. If it does, you have done something wrong and must correct this.
Only includes results that have actually been run and saved in the logs. Do not hallucinate results that don't exist.

results.claim: Average API cost per workflow with a gpt-4o backend is $2.33.
results.setup: Full workflow (7 subtasks), gpt-4o backend, Table 1 settings (3 mle-solver steps, 5 paper-solver steps); runs and mode not stated; cost is the API bill only
results.quote: Monetary costs per workflow were also substantially lower for gpt-4o, which averaged just $2.33 for the entire process.

results.claim: o1-mini and o1-preview cost $7.51 and $13.10 per workflow.
results.setup: Same workflow; o1-mini $7.51, o1-preview $13.10
results.quote: such as o1-mini at $7.51, and o1-preview at $13.10

results.claim: The 84% saving is against The AI Scientist's ~$15 (taken from Lu et al., not rerun) and holds for gpt-4o only.
results.setup: gpt-4o backend vs Lu et al. 2024b cost; o1-preview at $13.10 is only ~13% below $15 (reader arithmetic)
results.quote: which cost around ∼$15 (6.4x more expensive) to complete using gpt-4o

results.claim: Report Writing is the costliest phase for gpt-4o and o1-preview; for o1-mini Data Preparation is $3.03 vs Report Writing $2.58.
results.setup: o1-preview Report Writing; per-phase averages
results.note: Text says Report Writing is most expensive 'across models' but o1-mini Data Preparation ($3.03) exceeds its Report Writing ($2.58).
results.quote: $0.30 and $9.58 for o1-preview

results.claim: Wall-clock time per workflow: gpt-4o 1165.4 s, o1-mini 3616.8 s, o1-preview 6201.3 s.
results.setup: Whole workflow, M3 Max laptop, API inference
results.note: Per-phase times for gpt-4o and o1-preview sum to ~1181.9 s and ~6234.5 s (reader arithmetic from Fig 8 image), not the stated totals.
results.quote: completing the entire workflow in 1165.4 seconds, approximately 3.2x faster than o1-mini and 5.3x faster than o1-preview, which required 3616.8 seconds and 6201.3 seconds

results.claim: Mean subtask success rate is highest for o1-preview.
results.setup: Mean over subtasks, not end-to-end completion; gpt-4o 94.3, o1-mini 92.8
results.quote: o1-preview achieving the highest average subtask success rate (95.7%)

results.claim: Literature review phase had the lowest success rates.
results.setup: gpt-4o 60%, o1-mini 70%, o1-preview 80%
results.note: Text calls 60/70/80 a failure rate; Fig 8 labels them success rates (reader read of image). Ambiguous.
results.quote: the literature review phase had a high rate of failure, at 60%, 70%, and 80% for gpt-4o, o1-mini, and o1-preview respectively.

results.claim: Automated NeurIPS-style reviewer scores autonomous papers far above human reviewers.
results.setup: 15 autonomous papers (5 topics x 3 backends); LLM reviewer adapted from Lu et al. vs human reviewers; human mean 3.8/10
results.quote: While the automated reviewers gave an average overall above average NeurIPS paper score of 6.1/10, human reviewers provided a much lower average of 3.8/10 (-2.3 points).

results.claim: Human overall scores by backend: 3.5 (gpt-4o), 3.8 (o1-mini), 4.0 (o1-preview).
results.setup: Human reviewers, autonomous mode, o1-preview backend
results.quote: average overall ratings ranging from 3.5/10 with gpt-4o, 3.8/10 with o1-mini, and 4.0/10 with o1-preview.

results.claim: Autonomous papers fall 2.05 points below the average accepted NeurIPS 2024 paper.
results.setup: Benchmark from papercopilot.com statistics footnote; p.12 rounds it to 5.9
results.quote: NeurIPS 2024, which stands at 5.85∗(our scores were -2.05 points lower on average)

results.claim: Human automated clarity gap: automated 3.6/4 vs human 2.4/4.
results.setup: Same 15 papers
results.quote: automated reviewers rated clarity at 3.6/4 on average compared to 2.4/4 by human evaluators

results.claim: gpt-4o human ratings of experiment quality 2.6, report 3.0, usefulness 4.0 (1-5).
results.setup: 10 volunteer PhD students rated 3 random papers each, autonomous mode
results.quote: an average experimental quality rating of 2.6/5, a report quality rating of 3.0/5, and a usefulness rating of 4.0/5

results.claim: o1-mini has the highest experiment quality rating.
results.setup: Autonomous mode, 1-5 scale; report 3.2, usefulness 4.3
results.quote: with an average score of 3.2/5 (+0.6)

results.claim: o1-preview rated most useful.
results.setup: Autonomous mode, 1-5 scale; report 3.4, experiment 2.9
results.quote: averaging 4.4/5 (+0.4 from gpt-4o and +0.1 from o1-mini)

results.claim: Co-pilot papers rated higher by external evaluators than autonomous papers, but still below NeurIPS average.
results.setup: o1-mini for all phases except literature review; two papers per researcher; number of researchers and external evaluators not stated
results.quote: co-pilot overall scores, which average at 4.38, are still -1.45 points below the average score of 5.85 for an accepted paper at NeurIPS 2024

results.claim: Overall gain of co-pilot over autonomous is +0.58 (quality +0.75, soundness +0.48).
results.setup: External evaluators; autonomous baseline pools backends
results.quote: the largest improvements were seen for quality, which increased by +0.75, soundness, which improved by +0.48, and the overall score, which improved by +0.58.

results.claim: Self-evaluation of co-pilot papers is 4.13/10, lower than external 4.38/10.
results.setup: Researchers rated their own co-pilot papers
results.quote: with an overall average of 4.38/10, up from 4.13/10 in self-evaluations

results.claim: Co-pilot raters gave lower experiment quality (2.38) than autonomous o1-mini raters.
results.setup: Co-pilot, report 3.13, usefulness 3.75; different raters and papers
results.note: Deltas vs autonomous o1-mini: report -0.07, usefulness -0.55, experiment -0.82.
results.quote: We report an average experimental quality rating of 2.38/5, a report quality rating of 3.13/5, and a usefulness rating of

results.claim: Co-pilot tool ratings: utility 3.5, continuation 3.75, satisfaction 3.63, usability 4.0 (1-5).
results.setup: Self-report after two sessions; 75% answered optional feedback
results.quote: the overall scores across all experiments are 3.5/5 for utility, 3.75/5 for continuation, 3.63/5 for satisfaction, and 4.0/5 for usability

results.claim: mle-solver earned four medals on 10 low-complexity text/tabular MLE-Bench tasks vs OpenHands 2, AIDE 2, MLAB 0.
results.setup: 10 of MLE-Bench's 75 challenges; scored on 20% dev split not LLM reward; comparators MLAB/OpenHands gpt-4o, AIDE o1-preview; invalid comparator submissions excluded; mle-solver backend and run count not stated
results.quote: mle-solver obtaining four medals (two gold, one silver, and one bronze) compared with OpenHands (gpt-4o) obtaining two medals (two gold), AIDE (o1-preview) obtaining two medals (one gold, one bronze) and MLAB obtaining zero medals.

results.claim: mle-solver beats the human median on six of ten tasks.
results.setup: Same MLE-Bench subset; AIDE 5/10, OpenHands 2/10, MLAB 0/10 per text
results.note: Reader found Fig 9 shows 6 ticks for AIDE (image), tying mle-solver; text says 5.
results.quote: obtained above median human performance on six out of ten benchmarks, with AIDE obtaining five out of ten, OpenHands two out of ten, and MLAB zero out of ten.

results.claim: Lu et al. automated reviewer reached 65% accuracy vs 66% human on 500 ICLR 2022 papers (validation cited, not rerun).
results.setup: Reported from Lu et al. 2024b; F1 0.57 vs 0.49 after calibration
results.quote: the automated reviewer achieved human-level accuracy (65% compared to 66% for human reviewers) and surpassed human performance in F1 score (0.57 vs. 0.49)

results.claim: Without a limit, arXiv search by paper-solver could take up to 100 tries; limit set to 5.
results.setup: Observed failure mode, no frequency given
results.quote: it could take up to 100 tries for a successful search query to return any papers. A limit of 5 was place thereafter

limits: Reports are less satisfying than The AI Scientist's (lower quality figures) despite higher automated scores (p.19)
Reports not meant to replace human paper writing but NeurIPS scores are the quality heuristic (p.19)
Fixed section structure, max two figures, no repository-level code (pp.19-20)
Hallucinated experimental details in gpt-4o papers (p.20)
No significance tests, CIs or SDs; rater counts for co-pilot not stated; raters not blinded to AI authorship
Pipeline starts from a human-given idea; no ideation tested; ML topics only
Cost $2.33 is gpt-4o autonomous API cost only; co-pilot ran on o1-mini; human labour and failed runs not costed
Dated: gpt-4o, o1-mini, o1-preview backends and their prices
